title: Central sensitization
objective: Distinguish central from peripheral sensitization and define allodynia and hyperalgesia.

steps.title: Turning up the amplifier
steps.body: **[[central sensitization]]** is increased gain in the [[dorsal horn]] itself: after strong or sustained input, dorsal-horn neurons become more excitable. ('Wind-up' — a build-up of firing during repeated input — is a related but shorter-lived phenomenon that can help trigger it.) Now even normal touch input can be read as painful.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Pain from a normally non-painful stimulus
Exaggerated pain from a painful stimulus
steps.explanation: Allodynia = a gentle touch hurts; hyperalgesia = a painful stimulus hurts more than it should. Both can arise from central sensitization.

steps.setup: After an injury heals, light brushing of nearby, uninjured skin is painful.
steps.prompt: What best explains pain spreading beyond the injured area?
options: Central sensitization — the dorsal horn's gain is raised, so touch input reads as pain
The brush is causing fresh micro-damage to the skin each time it passes
Nociceptors have sprouted into the neighbouring uninjured skin
Only peripheral sensitization confined to the original injured site
steps.reveal: Pain in *uninjured* neighboring skin points to a central change: the dorsal horn amplifies even Aβ touch input (allodynia). Purely peripheral sensitization would stay confined to the inflamed tissue.

variants.prompt: Pain from light touch of uninjured skin near an old injury suggests…
options: Only peripheral sensitization at the old site
variants.explanation: Spread to uninjured skin and pain from touch point to a central, not purely peripheral, change.

steps.title: Two levels, one experience
steps.body: Peripheral sensitization turns up the *ending*; central sensitization turns up the *relay*. Chronic pain usually involves both. Touch-evoked pain (allodynia) in particular leans on the central side — which is why peripheral fixes alone often fall short.
